newsitem.title: USA: Texaco scandal encourages new plaintiffs.
newsitem.headline: Texaco scandal encourages new plaintiffs.

text.p: Texaco Inc.'s discrimination scandal is generating a ripple effect with an increasing number of potential plaintiffs working at other companies seeking to press claims against their employers, lawyers say.

Daniel Berger, one of the lawyers who sued Texaco on behalf of black claimants, said his firm, Bernstein Litowitz Berger & Grossmann, has been receiving about 10 calls a day from employees at other companies since news broke about taped racist remarks by former Texaco officials.
"This has energised a lot of people to come forward," Berger said. "I think you will see many more companies willing to settle discrimination cases."

Coincidentally, Lockheed Martin Corp. announced Thursday it had agreed to pay $13 million to settle one of the nation's biggest age discrimination lawsuits, affecting 2,000 former employees of the Martin Marietta Corp.
The Texaco scandal relates to a 1994 discrimination suit brought by a group of black plaintiffs who alleged the company systematically discriminated against them and denied them promotions.

Early this month plantiffs in that case asked a court to sanction Texaco because the claimants had acquired secret tapes of company executives discussing plans to destroy evidence of alleged discrimination as well as making racist remarks.
Transcripts of the tapes, which included profanities and the terms "niggers" and "black jelly beans," were filed as part of the court records.

After the contents of the tapes were widely publicised, Texaco agreed to settle the suit by paying $176.1 million and setting up an "equality and tolerance" task force with extraordinary powers to shape personnel policies and practices.

The tapes also led federal prosecutors to file a criminal obstruction of justice charge against Richard Lundwall, the former Texaco executive who made the tapes and eventually turned them over to the plaintiffs. Lundwall was one of the men heard on the tape discussing plans to destroy evidence.

Although federal guidelines allow for criminal obstruction of justice charges to be brought in civil cases where evidence is hidden or destroyed, defence lawyers said those charges are usually brought after a defendant has ignored a court order or subpoena requiring production of those documents.
No such order was in effect in the Texaco case and some lawyers believe the government will be trying to make new law with the case.

"It's a stretch as far as I'm concerned. I think the government is trying to carve out new ground," said James Linn, a prominent defence lawyer whose clients include former Philippine first lady Imelda Marcos.

Regardless of the outcome of the criminal investigation, lawyers specialising in employment cases said it only serves to heighten the awareness of discrimination by corporate America and the seriousness of civil lawsuits brought by minorities and women.

Judith Vladeck, a prominent plaintiffs discrimination lawyer with New York's Vladeck, Waldman, Elias & Engelhard, said the Texaco scandal will give credibility to existing discrimination cases and also encourage new plaintiffs to come forward.
"There's been such a powerful propoganda machine at work in the last 10 years saying that all of this is history," Vladeck said.

"But I think the Texaco case as well as the cases involving women employees in the financial industry demonstrate these problem remain universal and that all the little booklets given out by employers saying 'we will not tolerate discrimination' aren't worth the paper they are written on," she said.
She said that for too long human resource staffers have been trained to tell employees who complain of discrimination that they are emotionally disturbed or have interpersonal problems.
"Maybe now the HR people will be trained to be a little more sympathic. The potential for huge liability is a wonderfully educational tool," Vladeck said.
